title: API products, and gateways compared
summary: Many services behind one address, bundles for partners, the path-collision trap, and WSO2 versus APISIX versus Kong.

steps.title: One gateway, many services
body: A platform publishes **one API per service** on **one gateway address**:
```text
https://api.acme.example/catalogue/v1/books/{isbn}     → catalogue integration (transform)
https://api.acme.example/orders/v1/orders              → orders integration (mediation)
https://api.acme.example/shipping-rates/v1/quote       → shipping-rates service (pass-through)
- The **context** (`/catalogue`) is a **business noun**, never a system name: systems get replaced, consumers stay.
- Version **per service**: orders v2 ships without touching catalogue v1.
- Resources are **relative**: `/catalogue/v1/books/{isbn}`, not `/catalogue/v1/catalogue/books/...`.
- Keep each API small (a handful of operations). One API with dozens of resources means every change risks all of them.

steps.prompt: Which context is the best choice for the API in front of the warehouse system the shop calls "inventory"?
steps.explain: Name the business capability. When the warehouse system is replaced, `/inventory` still makes sense and no consumer has to change.

steps.title: API products
body: Sometimes a partner should see **one** API, not three. An **API product** bundles **selected operations** from
several APIs under **one context** and **one subscription**:
```text
/partner/v1/books/{isbn}     → from catalogue v1
/partner/v1/orders           → from orders v1
/partner/v1/quote            → from shipping-rates v1
Each operation still goes to its own backend; only the packaging changes. The catch: paths are **flattened**
under one context, so two operations that were distinct in their own APIs can **collide**. `GET /{isbn}` from
catalogue and `GET /{orderId}` from orders both become `GET /partner/v1/{x}`, and the gateway will route
every such call to whichever it matches first. Design distinctive paths (`/books/{isbn}`, `/orders/{id}`).

steps.prompt: A product includes catalogue's `GET /{isbn}` and orders' `GET /{orderId}`. A partner calls `GET /partner/v1/A1` for an order and gets `400 INVALID_REQUEST` from the catalogue integration. What happened?
options: The two templates collide after flattening; the gateway routed the call to catalogue, whose ISBN validation rejected it
steps.explain: Validation in the integration saved the backend from garbage (defence in depth), but the real fix is distinctive paths.

steps.title: Gateways compared, at a high level
body: | | **WSO2 API Manager** | **Apache APISIX** | **Kong Gateway** |

| Shape | full API management: gateway, key manager, publisher, developer portal, admin | a fast gateway (NGINX/OpenResty, config in etcd) with many plugins | a fast gateway (NGINX/OpenResty) with plugins; management features in paid tiers |
| OpenAPI import, portal | built in | limited; dashboard is basic | developer portal and management mostly in the enterprise product |
| OAuth key manager | built in (or external IdP) | delegates to an IdP such as Keycloak (`openid-connect` plugin) | plugins; usually an external IdP |
| Rate limiting | tiers, plans, traffic manager | `limit-count`, `limit-req` plugins | `rate-limiting` plugins |
| Configured via | portals, REST APIs, `apictl` | Admin API (JSON), declarative YAML | Admin API, declarative `deck` |
Cloud services (Azure API Management, AWS API Gateway, Google Apigee) offer the same concepts as managed services.
When choosing, check **current** licensing and patch policy (what security fixes the free edition gets, and when),
whether a portal and role-based access are included, and how well it fits your pipelines.

steps.prompt: Match the need to the product feature.
pairs: Partners must self-serve keys and read docs
An external key manager (Keycloak, Entra ID)
Promote API definitions from a pipeline
Protect a fragile backend from everyone together

foreach (var g in ops.GroupBy(o => o.Item2.Split(' ')[0] + " " + Shape(o.Item2.Split(' ')[1])))
steps.explain: Normalise parameter names away, and identical shapes reveal the collision.

steps.title: Find product collisions
prompt: The tests declare `record ProductOp(string Api, string Method, string Path);` (paths are relative to the product context).

Write `List<string> Collisions(List<ProductOp> ops)`. Two operations **collide** when they have the same method (ignore case) and the same number of segments, and at every position the segments are equal (ignore case) **or at least one of them is a `{parameter}`** (a parameter matches any literal, so `/{isbn}` and `/search` collide too).
Return one line per colliding pair, in input order (`i < j`): `"{METHOD} {path1} ({api1}) vs {path2} ({api2})"` with the method upper-cased.
solution: var x = Seg(a.Path); var y = Seg(b.Path);
for (int j = i + 1; j < ops.Count; j++)
hints: Compare every pair `i < j` with a local `Collide(a, b)` function.
A position is fine if either side is a parameter or the literals are equal.
template: Dojo.Eq("distinctive paths don't collide", new List<string>(), Collisions(dojoGood));
record ProductOp(string Api, string Method, string Path);
